reminder: In a Dedekind domain, every nonzero proper ideal is a product of prime ideals.
definition: A Dedekind domain is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) in which every nonzero proper [ideal](c:ideal) is a product of [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal). Equivalently, it is a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) that is an [integrally closed domain](c:integrally-closed-domain) in which every nonzero prime ideal is maximal.
examples: The ring $\mathbb Z$ and the polynomial ring $k[x]$ over a field $k$ are Dedekind domains, because every [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) is one.
The [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) of a [number field](c:number-field) is a Dedekind domain. For example, $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is one, and it is not a principal ideal domain.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is not a Dedekind domain. The number $(1+\sqrt{-3})/2$ is integral over it but lies outside it, so the ring is not integrally closed.

steps: Take a Dedekind domain $R$.
By definition, $R$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
The Dedekind condition adds that every nonzero proper ideal of $R$ factors into prime ideals.
links.why: Every fact about integral domains holds in a Dedekind domain, which has the extra property of unique ideal factorization.

steps: Take a principal ideal domain $R$ and a nonzero proper ideal $(a)$, so $a$ is a nonzero nonunit.
A principal ideal domain is a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain), so $a=p_1\cdots p_n$ with irreducible elements $p_i$.
Each $(p_i)$ is a prime ideal, and $(a)=(p_1)\cdots(p_n)$.
So $R$ is a Dedekind domain, but a Dedekind domain can have ideals that are not principal.
links.why: Results about Dedekind domains apply to $\mathbb Z$ and to polynomial rings over a field, which are the standard principal ideal domains.

reminder: The Dedekind zeta function of a number field sums $N(\mathfrak a)^{-s}$ over all nonzero ideals $\mathfrak a$ of its ring of integers.
definition: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal O_K$. Its Dedekind zeta function is $\zeta_K(s)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}N(\mathfrak a)^{-s}$, where $\mathfrak a$ runs over the nonzero [ideals](c:ideal) of $\mathcal O_K$ and $N(\mathfrak a)=|\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak a|$. The series converges for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, and $\zeta_K$ extends by [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) to a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on $\mathbb C$ with one simple pole at $s=1$.
examples: For $K=\mathbb Q$, the nonzero ideals are $n\mathbb Z$ with norm $n$, so $\zeta_{\mathbb Q}$ is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function).
For $K=\mathbb Q(i)$, one has $\zeta_K(s)=\zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-4})$, and the residue of $\zeta_K$ at $s=1$ is $\pi/4$.

Non-example: the sum of $|N(\alpha)|^{-s}$ over nonzero elements $\alpha$ of $\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ diverges for every $s$, because each ideal has infinitely many generators. The Dedekind zeta function sums over ideals.

steps: Take $K=\mathbb Q$, so $\mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z$.
Every nonzero ideal of $\mathbb Z$ is $n\mathbb Z$ with $n\ge1$, and its norm is $n$.
So the sum over ideals becomes $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$, which is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function).
links.why: Facts about the Riemann zeta function, such as the Euler product and the pole at $s=1$, carry over to every number field.

steps: For each $n\ge1$, let $a_n$ be the number of nonzero ideals of $\mathcal O_K$ with norm $n$.
Grouping the ideals by norm gives $\zeta_K(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_nn^{-s}$.
This is a [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) with coefficients $a_n$.
The number field adds that the coefficients count ideals, which gives an Euler product over prime ideals.
links.why: General facts about convergence of Dirichlet series give the half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ where the Dedekind zeta function converges.

reminder: A density matrix is a positive operator of trace one on a Hilbert space.
definition: A density matrix on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a [positive operator](c:positive-operator) $\rho$ of [trace class](c:trace-class-operator) with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. It describes a mixed [quantum state](c:quantum-state), and the expected value of an observable $A$ in this state is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$.
examples: For a unit vector $\psi$, the projection $|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ is a density matrix. It describes a [pure state](c:pure-state).
On $\mathbb C^2$, the matrix $\tfrac12I$ is the [maximally mixed state](c:maximally-mixed-quantum-state), and $\operatorname{diag}(p,1-p)$ mixes two pure states with weights $p$ and $1-p$.
Non-example: the identity matrix $I$ on $\mathbb C^2$ is positive but has trace $2$, so it is not a density matrix. The matrix $\tfrac12I$ is one.

steps: Take a unit vector $\psi$ in $H$ and the projection $P=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$.
The operator $P$ is positive, and its trace is $\|\psi\|^2=1$.
So $P$ is a density matrix, and it is the matrix of the [pure state](c:pure-state) $\psi$.
A general density matrix is a convex combination of such projections, which is a mixed state.
links.why: A learner can read a pure state as a rank-one density matrix and use one formalism for pure and mixed states.

steps: Take a Hilbert space $H$ of finite dimension $n$.
The operator $I/n$ is positive and has trace $1$.
So $I/n$ is a density matrix, namely the [maximally mixed state](c:maximally-mixed-quantum-state).
A general density matrix need not be a multiple of the identity.
links.why: The maximally mixed state is the most symmetric density matrix, which makes a good test case.

reminder: A diagram in a category is a functor from a small index category into it.
definition: A diagram of shape $J$ in a [category](c:category) $C$ is a [functor](c:functor) $D:J\to C$ from a [small category](c:small-category) $J$. It chooses an object $D(j)$ of $C$ for each object $j$ of $J$ and a morphism $D(u)$ for each arrow $u$ of $J$.
examples: A parallel pair $f,g:A\rightrightarrows B$ is a diagram. Its shape has two objects and two parallel arrows.
A square of four objects and four morphisms is a diagram of shape $[1]\times[1]$. It is a [commutative diagram](c:commutative-diagram) when the two composites agree.
A sequence $X_0\to X_1\to X_2\to\cdots$ is a diagram whose shape is the poset $(\mathbb N,\le)$.
Non-example: the identity functor $\mathrm{Set}\to\mathrm{Set}$ is not a diagram in this sense, because its source $\mathrm{Set}$ is not small.

steps: Take a diagram $D:J\to C$.
By definition, $D$ is a [functor](c:functor) from $J$ to $C$.
The diagram adds that $J$ is a small index category, chosen to draw a pattern of objects and arrows in $C$.
links.why: Everything known about functors applies to diagrams, and the index category $J$ records the shape of a limit or colimit.

steps: Take a commutative diagram of objects and morphisms in $C$.
Read its arrows as a functor $D:J\to C$, where $J$ is the category generated by the arrows subject to the commuting relations.
So the commutative diagram is a diagram of shape $J$.
A general diagram need not commute, because its shape $J$ can be the free category on a graph.
links.why: A commutative diagram is a diagram whose shape forces equal composites, so limit and colimit language applies to it.

steps: Take a directed set $(I,\le)$ and view it as a category with one arrow $i\to j$ when $i\le j$.
A [directed system](c:directed-system) in $C$ is a functor $I\to C$.
So it is a diagram of shape $I$.
The directed case adds that every two indices have a common upper bound.
links.why: A directed system is a diagram over a directed poset, so its colimit is a colimit of a diagram.

reminder: The difference quotient of $f$ at two points $x$ and $y$ is $(f(x)-f(y))/(x-y)$, the slope of a secant line.
definition: Let $f$ be a [function](c:function) from a subset $S$ of a [field](c:field) $F$ into $F$. For $x,y\in S$ with $x\ne y$, the difference quotient of $f$ is $\dfrac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}$. With $y=x+h$ it is $\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$, the slope of the [secant](c:secant) through $(x,f(x))$ and $(y,f(y))$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$, the difference quotient is $x+y$, because $(x^2-y^2)/(x-y)=x+y$.
For $f(x)=3x+1$, every difference quotient equals $3$.
For a differentiable function, the difference quotient tends to the [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$ as $y$ tends to $x$.
Non-example: at a pair with $x=y$, the expression $(f(x)-f(x))/(x-x)$ is $0/0$, so no difference quotient exists there.

reminder: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation with integer coefficients whose integer solutions are sought.
definition: A Diophantine equation is an [equation](c:equation) $P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0$ where $P$ is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [integer](c:integer) coefficients. A solution is a tuple of integers (sometimes of [rational numbers](c:rational-number)) that satisfies it.
examples: The equation $x^2+y^2=z^2$ has the integer solution $(3,4,5)$.
The [Pell equation](c:pell-equation) $x^2-2y^2=1$ has the solutions $(3,2)$ and $(17,12)$.
The equation $x^2+y^2=3$ has no integer solution, because a sum of two squares is never $3$ modulo $4$.
Non-example: $2^x=y+1$ has the unknown $x$ in an exponent, so it is not a polynomial equation. It is an [exponential Diophantine equation](c:exponential-diophantine-equation).

steps: Take a Diophantine equation $P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0$.
Since $P$ is a polynomial, this is an [algebraic equation](c:algebraic-equation).
The Diophantine case adds that the coefficients are integers and the solutions sought are integers or rational numbers.
links.why: Tools for algebraic equations, such as reduction modulo $m$, apply to Diophantine equations, which ask for integral solutions.

steps: Take the [Pell equation](c:pell-equation) $x^2-dy^2=1$ with a positive integer $d$ that is not a square.
It has the form $P(x,y)=0$ with $P=x^2-dy^2-1$, a polynomial with integer coefficients.
So it is a Diophantine equation, and it asks for integer solutions $(x,y)$.
The Pell equation adds a fixed quadratic form, which gives infinitely many solutions.
links.why: Pell's equation is the standard example of a Diophantine equation that has an infinite solution family.

reminder: Two subsets of a set are disjoint when they have no common element.
definition: Two [subsets](c:subset) $A$ and $B$ of a set are disjoint when their [intersection](c:intersection) is the [empty subset](c:empty-subset), that is, $A\cap B=\varnothing$. Equivalently, no [element](c:element) lies in both $A$ and $B$.
examples: The even integers and the odd integers are disjoint subsets of $\mathbb Z$.
The empty set is disjoint from every set, including itself.
Non-example: $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ are not disjoint, because $3$ lies in both.

reminder: Dolbeault cohomology of a complex manifold is the cohomology of the complex of $(p,q)$-forms with the operator $\bar\partial$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) with its [Dolbeault complex](c:dolbeault-complex) of smooth $(p,q)$-forms $\mathcal A^{p,q}(X)$ and operator $\bar\partial$. The Dolbeault cohomology is $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X)=\ker(\bar\partial:\mathcal A^{p,q}\to\mathcal A^{p,q+1})/\operatorname{im}(\bar\partial:\mathcal A^{p,q-1}\to\mathcal A^{p,q})$. It is the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of this complex in each bidegree.
examples: On the projective line $\mathbb{CP}^1$, one has $H^{0,0}=\mathbb C$, $H^{0,1}=0$ and $H^{1,1}=\mathbb C$.
On a complex torus $\mathbb C/\Lambda$, the group $H^{0,1}$ has dimension $1$ and is spanned by the class of $d\bar z$.
Non-example: the de Rham cohomology $H^1_{dR}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)$ has dimension $2$. It uses $d$ and not $\bar\partial$, so it is not Dolbeault cohomology.

steps: Take the Dolbeault complex $\mathcal A^{p,\bullet}(X)$ with differential $\bar\partial$, which satisfies $\bar\partial^2=0$.
This is a cochain complex of complex vector spaces.
Its [cohomology](c:cohomology) in degree $q$ is the kernel of $\bar\partial$ modulo the image of $\bar\partial$, which is $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X)$.
links.why: General tools for cohomology, such as long exact sequences, apply to Dolbeault cohomology.

reminder: A duality between two categories is an equivalence from one category to the opposite of the other.
definition: A duality between [categories](c:category) $C$ and $D$ is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) $C\simeq D^{\mathrm{op}}$ with the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) of $D$. Equivalently, it is a [contravariant functor](c:contravariant-functor) $C\to D$ that is fully faithful and essentially surjective.
examples: [Stone duality](c:stone-duality) says that the category of [Boolean algebras](c:boolean-algebra) is dual to the category of [Stone spaces](c:stone-space).
Finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $k$ are dual to themselves by the functor $V\mapsto V^*$.
Non-example: the category $\mathrm{Set}$ is not dual to itself, because $\mathrm{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$ is not equivalent to $\mathrm{Set}$.

steps: Take a duality between $C$ and $D$.
By definition, it is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) between $C$ and $D^{\mathrm{op}}$.
So it is an equivalence of categories in which the target is an opposite category.
The duality adds that arrows change direction when read from $D$.
links.why: Facts about equivalences, such as preservation of limits, turn into facts that exchange limits and colimits.

steps: Take the categories of Boolean algebras and of Stone spaces.
Sending a Boolean algebra to its space of ultrafilters is a contravariant functor to Stone spaces.
Sending a Stone space to its Boolean algebra of clopen sets is a contravariant inverse, up to isomorphism.
So the two categories are dual in the sense above.
links.why: Stone duality is the model example of a duality, so a learner can test the general notion on it.

reminder: An E-infinity ring is a spectrum with a multiplication that is commutative and associative up to coherent homotopy.
definition: An $E_\infty$ ring is an algebra over the [E-infinity operad](c:e-infinity-operad) in [spectra](c:spectrum-object) with the [smash product](c:smash-product-of-spectra). It is a spectrum $R$ with a unit and a multiplication $R\wedge R\to R$ that is associative and commutative up to a coherent system of higher homotopies. Its homotopy groups $\pi_*R$ form a graded-commutative ring.
examples: The [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) $\mathbb S$ and the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $HR$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ are $E_\infty$ rings.
Complex K-theory $KU$, the Thom spectrum $MU$ and the spectrum $\mathrm{tmf}$ of [topological modular forms](c:tmf) are $E_\infty$ rings.
Non-example: for the noncommutative ring $R=M_2(\mathbb Z)$, the spectrum $HR$ is an $A_\infty$ ring but not an $E_\infty$ ring, because $\pi_0(HR)=R$ is not commutative.

steps: Take a symmetric monoidal $(\infty,1)$-category, here spectra with the smash product.
An [E-infinity algebra](c:e-infinity-algebra) in it is an object with a multiplication that is commutative up to coherent homotopy.
For spectra, these algebras are exactly the $E_\infty$ rings.
links.why: General results on $E_\infty$ algebras, such as the existence of free algebras, apply to $E_\infty$ rings.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ and its Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HR$.
Because $R$ is commutative, the multiplication of $HR$ is commutative up to coherent homotopy.
So $HR$ is an $E_\infty$ ring with $\pi_0(HR)=R$.
An $E_\infty$ ring can also have nonzero higher homotopy groups.
links.why: Commutative rings sit inside $E_\infty$ rings, so algebra over a ring is the discrete case of algebra over an $E_\infty$ ring.

steps: Take an $E_\infty$ ring $R$ and forget the higher commutativity homotopies.
What remains is a multiplication that is associative up to coherent homotopy.
So $R$ is an [associative ring spectrum](c:associative-ring-spectrum), and the $E_\infty$ structure adds commutativity.
links.why: Every $E_\infty$ ring is a ring spectrum, so theorems about module spectra over ring spectra apply.

reminder: The edge density of a graph is the number of its edges divided by the number of possible edges.
definition: For a [finite graph](c:finite-graph) $G$ with $n\ge2$ [vertices](c:vertex) and $e(G)$ [edges](c:edge), the edge density is $d(G)=e(G)/\binom n2$. For disjoint vertex sets $A$ and $B$, the density of the pair is $d(A,B)=e(A,B)/(|A||B|)$, where $e(A,B)$ counts the edges with one end in $A$ and one end in $B$.
examples: The [complete graph](c:complete-graph) $K_n$ has density $1$, and a graph with no edges has density $0$.
The $5$-cycle has $5$ edges out of $\binom52=10$ possible edges, so its density is $1/2$.
In the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,m}$ with sides $A$ and $B$, the pair $(A,B)$ has density $1$.
Non-example: the average degree of a graph is not its edge density. The $5$-cycle has average degree $2$ and density $1/2$.

reminder: An elementary substructure satisfies every first-order formula with parameters from it exactly as the larger structure does.
definition: Let $M$ be a [substructure](c:substructure) of a [first-order structure](c:structure) $N$. Then $M$ is an elementary substructure of $N$, written $M\preceq N$, when $M\models\varphi(\bar a)$ if and only if $N\models\varphi(\bar a)$ for every [first-order formula](c:formula) $\varphi(\bar x)$ and every tuple $\bar a$ from $M$.
examples: The rational numbers $(\mathbb Q,<)$ form an elementary substructure of $(\mathbb R,<)$, because both are dense linear orders without endpoints.
The real algebraic numbers form an elementary substructure of the ordered field $\mathbb R$, because the theory of real closed fields is model complete.
Non-example: $(\mathbb N,<)$ is a substructure of $(\mathbb Z,<)$ but not an elementary one. The formula $\exists y\,(y<x)$ is false for $x=0$ in $\mathbb N$ and true in $\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take an elementary substructure $M\preceq N$.
By definition, $M$ is a [substructure](c:substructure) of $N$.
Quantifier-free formulas already agree on $M$ and $N$ for every substructure.
The elementary case adds that formulas with quantifiers also agree on tuples from $M$.
links.why: A learner sees that elementarity is exactly the extra agreement on quantified formulas that a plain substructure lacks.

steps: Take the inclusion map $i:M\to N$ of an elementary substructure, so $i(a)=a$.
For every formula $\varphi$ and tuple $\bar a$ from $M$, $M\models\varphi(\bar a)$ if and only if $N\models\varphi(\bar a)$.
So $i$ is an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding).
Conversely, the image of an elementary embedding into $N$ is an elementary substructure of $N$.
links.why: Elementary substructures are the inclusions among elementary embeddings, so results on embeddings give results on substructures.

reminder: An elliptic complex is a complex of differential operators whose symbols form an exact sequence at every nonzero covector.
definition: An elliptic complex on a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ is a sequence $0\to\Gamma(E_0)\xrightarrow{D_0}\Gamma(E_1)\xrightarrow{D_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{D_{N-1}}\Gamma(E_N)\to0$ of [differential operators](c:differential-operator) between sections of [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) with $D_{i+1}D_i=0$. It is elliptic when, for every nonzero cotangent vector $\xi$, the sequence of [symbols](c:symbol-of-a-differential-operator) $\sigma(D_i)(\xi)$ is exact.
examples: The [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex) of a manifold is elliptic. Its symbol sequence is the exact Koszul complex of wedge product with $\xi$.
The [Dolbeault complex](c:dolbeault-complex) of a complex manifold is elliptic.
Non-example: the complex $0\to C^\infty(M)\xrightarrow{0}C^\infty(M)\to0$ with the zero operator is not elliptic. Its symbol sequence $0\to\mathbb C\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb C\to0$ is not exact.

steps: Take an [elliptic operator](c:elliptic-operator) $D:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(F)$.
Form the two-term complex $0\to\Gamma(E)\xrightarrow{D}\Gamma(F)\to0$, which is a complex because no composite exists.
Its symbol sequence is exact at every $\xi\ne0$ exactly when $\sigma(D)(\xi)$ is an isomorphism.
So an elliptic operator is a two-term elliptic complex.
links.why: Index theory for elliptic operators is the two-term case of index theory for elliptic complexes.

steps: Take $E_k=\Lambda^kT^*M$ and $D_k=d$, so that $D_{k+1}D_k=d^2=0$.
The symbol of $d$ at $\xi\ne0$ is wedge product with $i\xi$.
The complex of these wedge maps is the Koszul complex, which is exact for $\xi\ne0$.
So the [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex) is an elliptic complex.
links.why: The de Rham complex is the first example of an elliptic complex, and Hodge theory for it follows the general pattern.

steps: Take the spaces $\Gamma(E_i)$ of sections with the maps $D_i$.
Because $D_{i+1}D_i=0$, this is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) of vector spaces.
An elliptic complex adds that the maps are differential operators and that the symbol sequence is exact.
links.why: Cohomology of an elliptic complex is ordinary cohomology of a cochain complex, and ellipticity makes it finite dimensional on compact manifolds.

reminder: The Shannon entropy of a probability distribution is $-\sum p_i\log p_i$, a measure of average uncertainty.
definition: Let $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ be a finite [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution). Its entropy is $H(p)=-\sum_{i=1}^np_i\log p_i$ with $0\log0=0$, where $\log$ is the [logarithm](c:logarithm) to a fixed base, and base $2$ gives bits. The entropy of a [random variable](c:random-variable) is the entropy of its distribution.
examples: A fair coin has $p=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and entropy $1$ bit. A fair die has entropy $\log_26$ bits.
A certain outcome $p=(1,0,\dots,0)$ has entropy $0$.
Among distributions on $n$ outcomes, the uniform one has the largest entropy, namely $\log n$.
Non-example: the number of outcomes is not the entropy. A coin with $p=(0.99,0.01)$ has two outcomes but entropy of about $0.08$ bits.

steps: For $\alpha\ne1$, the [Rényi entropy](c:renyi-entropy) is $H_\alpha(p)=\frac1{1-\alpha}\log\sum_ip_i^\alpha$.
Let $\alpha$ tend to $1$ and apply l'Hôpital's rule.
The limit is $-\sum_ip_i\log p_i$.
So the Shannon entropy is the Rényi entropy of order $1$.
links.why: Shannon entropy is the order-one member of the Rényi family, next to min-entropy and max-entropy.

reminder: A probability measure preserved by a map is ergodic when every invariant set has measure zero or one.
definition: Let $T$ be a map on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $X$ and let $\mu$ be a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $X$ that $T$ preserves, so that $T$ is a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map). The measure $\mu$ is ergodic for $T$ when every measurable set $A$ with $T^{-1}A=A$ has $\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}$.
examples: The rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha$ of the circle $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with Lebesgue measure is ergodic when $\alpha$ is irrational.
The doubling map $x\mapsto2x\bmod1$ on $[0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure is ergodic.
Every Bernoulli shift with its product measure is ergodic.
Non-example: the identity map of $[0,1]$ preserves Lebesgue measure, but the invariant set $[0,\tfrac12]$ has measure $\tfrac12$. So the measure is not ergodic.

steps: Take an ergodic measure $\mu$ for a map $T$.
By definition, $T$ preserves $\mu$, so $\mu$ is an [invariant measure](c:invariant-measure).
Ergodicity adds that every invariant measurable set has measure $0$ or $1$.
links.why: Ergodic measures are the indecomposable invariant probability measures, so every invariant measure is built from them.

reminder: Étale cohomology is the sheaf cohomology of a scheme computed on its étale site.
definition: For a [scheme](c:scheme) $X$, let $X_{et}$ be its [étale site](c:etale-site). The étale cohomology $H^i_{et}(X,F)$ of an étale sheaf $F$ of abelian groups is the $i$-th [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology), that is, the $i$-th right derived functor of global sections on $X_{et}$. For a prime $\ell$ invertible on $X$, the groups $H^i_{et}(X,\mathbb Z/\ell^n)$ form an inverse system whose limit gives the $\ell$-adic cohomology $H^i(X,\mathbb Z_\ell)$.
examples: For $X=\operatorname{Spec}k$ with $k$ a field, $H^i_{et}(X,F)$ is the [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology) of $\operatorname{Gal}(k^{sep}/k)$ with coefficients in $F$.
For a smooth projective curve $C$ of genus $g$ over an algebraically closed field, and $\ell$ invertible, $H^1_{et}(C,\mathbb Z_\ell)$ is free of rank $2g$.

Non-example: Zariski cohomology of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Z/\ell$ on an irreducible variety vanishes in positive degrees, so it does not see the topology. Étale cohomology of an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field, with $\ell$ invertible, has $H^1\cong(\mathbb Z/\ell)^2$.

steps: Take the étale site of $X$, which is a [Grothendieck site](c:grothendieck-site).
Take the category of étale sheaves of abelian groups on this site.
Derive the global sections functor on this category.
The derived functors are [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) on the étale site, and this is étale cohomology.
links.why: Étale cohomology is sheaf cohomology for a topology finer than the Zariski topology, so general tools for derived functors apply.

steps: Take a field $k$ and $X=\operatorname{Spec}k$.
The étale $X$-schemes are disjoint unions of spectra of finite separable extensions of $k$.
So étale sheaves on $X$ are discrete modules over $G=\operatorname{Gal}(k^{sep}/k)$, and global sections become $G$-invariants.
Their derived functors are the group cohomology of $G$, which is [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology).
links.why: Galois cohomology is étale cohomology of a point, so étale cohomology extends it to arbitrary schemes.

reminder: The Euclidean algorithm finds a greatest common divisor by replacing a pair $(a,b)$ with $(b,r)$, where $r$ is the remainder.
definition: Let $R$ be a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain), such as $\mathbb Z$ or a polynomial ring over a field, with Euclidean function $\delta$. Given $a,b$ with $b\ne0$, the [algorithm](c:algorithm) writes $a=qb+r$ with $r=0$ or $\delta(r)<\delta(b)$, and repeats with the pair $(b,r)$. It stops when the remainder is $0$, and the last nonzero remainder is a [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of $a$ and $b$.
examples: In $\mathbb Q[x]$, divide $x^2-1$ by $x^2-3x+2$ to get remainder $3x-3$. Then $x^2-3x+2=(\tfrac13x-\tfrac23)(3x-3)$, so the gcd is $x-1$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z[x]$ is not a Euclidean domain, so division with remainder and the algorithm fail there. The ideal $(2,x)$ is not principal.

reminder: Euler's totient function $\varphi(n)$ counts the integers from $1$ to $n$ that are coprime to $n$.
definition: For a positive [integer](c:integer) $n$, $\varphi(n)$ is the number of integers $k$ with $1\le k\le n$ that are [coprime](c:coprime-integers) to $n$. It is the order of the [group of units](c:group-of-units) of $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. It satisfies $\varphi(n)=n\prod_{p\mid n}(1-1/p)$, where $p$ runs over the primes that divide $n$.
examples: $\varphi(12)=4$, because $1,5,7,11$ are the integers up to $12$ coprime to $12$.
For a prime $p$, $\varphi(p)=p-1$ and $\varphi(p^k)=p^k-p^{k-1}$.
$\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$ when $m,n$ are coprime, so $\varphi(35)=\varphi(5)\varphi(7)=24$.
Non-example: $\varphi$ is not multiplicative without coprimality. $\varphi(4)=2$ but $\varphi(2)\varphi(2)=1$.

steps: An [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function) is a function defined on the positive integers.
The rule $n\mapsto\varphi(n)$ assigns an integer to each positive integer, so it is one.
It adds that $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$ for coprime $m$ and $n$.
links.why: General tools for arithmetic functions, such as Dirichlet convolution, apply to $\varphi$, which is also multiplicative.

reminder: An exact functor sends every short exact sequence to a short exact sequence.
definition: An [additive functor](c:additive) $F:A\to B$ between [abelian categories](c:abelian-category) is exact when it sends every short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0\to X\to Y\to Z\to0$ to a short exact sequence $0\to FX\to FY\to FZ\to0$. Equivalently, $F$ preserves finite limits and finite colimits. It is left exact or right exact when it preserves only finite limits or only finite colimits.
examples: The forgetful functor from $R$-modules to abelian groups is exact.
Localization $S^{-1}(-)$ of $R$-modules is exact, and so is $-\otimes_RM$ when $M$ is flat, for example $-\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$.

Non-example: $-\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/2$ sends the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z$ to the zero map $\mathbb Z/2\to\mathbb Z/2$, which is not injective. It is right exact but not exact.

steps: Take an exact functor $F$ between abelian categories.
By definition, $F$ is an [additive functor](c:additive).
Exactness adds that $F$ keeps every short exact sequence exact.
links.why: An exact functor keeps all homological structure, such as kernels, cokernels and long exact sequences.

reminder: An exponential object $X^Y$ has an evaluation map such that maps $Z\times Y\to X$ correspond to maps $Z\to X^Y$.
definition: Let $C$ be a [category](c:category) with binary [products](c:product), and let $X$ and $Y$ be objects of $C$. An exponential object $X^Y$ comes with an evaluation morphism $\mathrm{ev}:X^Y\times Y\to X$ with this [universal property](c:universal-property): for every $f:Z\times Y\to X$ there is a unique $\tilde f:Z\to X^Y$ with $\mathrm{ev}\circ(\tilde f\times\mathrm{id}_Y)=f$.
examples: In $\mathrm{Set}$, the exponential $X^Y$ is the [set of functions](c:function-set) from $Y$ to $X$, and $\mathrm{ev}(f,y)=f(y)$.
In a Heyting algebra, viewed as a category, the exponential $X^Y$ is the implication $Y\Rightarrow X$.
In $\mathrm{Top}$, the space of continuous maps $Y\to X$ with the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology) is an exponential when $Y$ is locally compact Hausdorff.
Non-example: the rationals $\mathbb Q$ are not locally compact, so $-\times\mathbb Q$ has no right adjoint in $\mathrm{Top}$. The exponential $X^{\mathbb Q}$ fails to exist for some spaces $X$.

steps: Take a monoidal category whose tensor product is the categorical product.
An [internal hom](c:internal-hom) $[Y,X]$ has a natural bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(Z\times Y,X)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(Z,[Y,X])$.
This is the universal property of $X^Y$, so $X^Y=[Y,X]$.
The exponential object adds that the monoidal structure is the cartesian product.
links.why: Exponentials are internal homs for the cartesian product, so general results on closed monoidal categories apply.

steps: Take the category of sets, where products are cartesian products.
For sets $X$ and $Y$, let $X^Y$ be the set of functions $Y\to X$, with $\mathrm{ev}(f,y)=f(y)$.
A function $g:Z\times Y\to X$ corresponds to $\tilde g(z)=g(z,-)$, which is [currying](c:currying).
So the function set is the exponential object in $\mathrm{Set}$.
links.why: The exponential object carries the idea of a function set to any category, so currying holds in every cartesian closed category.

reminder: The exterior derivative $d$ maps $k$-forms to $(k+1)$-forms, extends the differential of functions, and satisfies $d^2=0$.
definition: On a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, the exterior derivative is the unique linear map $d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M)$ on [differential forms](c:differential-form) with three properties. It gives $df$, the [differential](c:differential) of every [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f$, it satisfies $d^2=0$, and it satisfies $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$ for a $k$-form $\alpha$. In coordinates, $d(f\,dx^I)=\sum_j\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\,dx^j\wedge dx^I$.
examples: For $f=x^2y$ on $\mathbb R^2$, $df=2xy\,dx+x^2\,dy$.
For $\alpha=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ on $\mathbb R^2$, $d\alpha=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\,dx\wedge dy$.
On $\mathbb R^3$, the operator $d$ on forms of degree $0$, $1$ and $2$ corresponds to the [gradient](c:gradient), the [curl](c:curl) and the [divergence](c:divergence).
Non-example: taking only the partial derivative of the coefficients is not $d$. For $y\,dx$ the partial derivative in $x$ gives $0$, but $d(y\,dx)=dy\wedge dx\ne0$.

steps: Take a smooth function $f$, which is a form of degree $0$.
By the first property, $df$ is the [differential](c:differential) of $f$, a $1$-form.
So on $0$-forms the exterior derivative is the differential.
On higher forms it adds the rules $d^2=0$ and the signed Leibniz rule.
links.why: The differential of a function is the first step of the de Rham complex, which the exterior derivative continues.

steps: Take a vector field $F=(P,Q,R)$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and the $1$-form $\alpha=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz$.
Compute $d\alpha=(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy$.
These coefficients are the components of $\operatorname{curl}F$.
So the [curl](c:curl) is $d$ on $1$-forms of $\mathbb R^3$, and $d$ works in every dimension.
links.why: Vector calculus identities such as $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{grad}=0$ are the single identity $d^2=0$.

reminder: A fibration is a map that has the homotopy lifting property.
definition: A continuous map $p:E\to B$ is a Hurewicz fibration when it has the [homotopy lifting property](c:homotopy-lifting-property) for all spaces $X$. Every [homotopy](c:homotopy) $H:X\times[0,1]\to B$ and every lift $\tilde h_0:X\to E$ of $H(-,0)$ then extend to a homotopy $\tilde H:X\times[0,1]\to E$ with $p\tilde H=H$. A Serre fibration needs this only for disks $X=D^n$.
examples: Every [covering space](c:covering-space) projection is a fibration with discrete fibres.
Every [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) is a Serre fibration, for example the Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$, and it is a Hurewicz fibration over a paracompact base.
For a pointed space $B$, the path fibration $PB\to B$, $\gamma\mapsto\gamma(1)$, is a fibration with fibre the loop space $\Omega B$.
Non-example: the inclusion $\{0\}\hookrightarrow[0,1]$ is not a fibration. The path $t\mapsto t$ starts at the image of $0$ but has no lift, because no point of $\{0\}$ lies over $t>0$.

steps: Take a covering map $p:E\to B$, a homotopy $H:X\times[0,1]\to B$ and a lift $\tilde h_0$ of $H(-,0)$.
For each $x$, the path $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ has a unique lift starting at $\tilde h_0(x)$.
These lifts together form a continuous homotopy $\tilde H$ with $p\tilde H=H$.
So $p$ has the homotopy lifting property, and the covering case adds discrete fibres and unique lifts.
links.why: A covering map is a fibration with discrete fibres, so the long exact sequence of homotopy groups applies to it.

steps: Take a fibre bundle $p:E\to B$ with paracompact base, so $E$ is locally a product $U\times F$ over open sets $U$.
Subdivide $X\times[0,1]$ so that each piece maps into one set $U$, where a lift exists by the product structure.
A partition of unity glues these local lifts into one lift over all of $B$.
So $p$ is a Hurewicz fibration, and over a general base the same idea gives a Serre fibration.
links.why: Bundles give most fibrations met in practice, so fibration results apply to them.

steps: Take the inclusion $i_0:X\to X\times[0,1]$ given by $x\mapsto(x,0)$.
A commutative square from $i_0$ to $p$ is a homotopy $H$ together with a lift $\tilde h_0$ of $H(-,0)$.
A diagonal filler of this square is a lifted homotopy $\tilde H$.
So a fibration is a map with the right lifting property against all inclusions $i_0$.
links.why: This view lets a learner define fibrations in any model category by lifting against a chosen class of maps.

reminder: A flag variety is the projective variety of chains of nested subspaces of a vector space.
definition: For a vector space $V$ of dimension $n$, the flag variety is the set of chains $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=V$ of [linear subspaces](c:linear-subspace) with $\dim V_i=i$. It is a [projective variety](c:projective-variety) inside a product of [Grassmannians](c:grassmannian). More generally, for a [reductive group](c:reductive-group) $G$ and a [parabolic subgroup](c:parabolic-subgroup) $P$, the generalized flag variety is the quotient $G/P$.
examples: For $n=2$, the flag variety of $k^2$ is the projective line $\mathbb P^1$, because a flag is just a line $V_1$ in $k^2$.
For $n=3$, the flag variety is the variety of pairs (point, line through it) in $\mathbb P^2$, of dimension $3$.
The Grassmannian of $k$-dimensional subspaces of $k^n$ is $GL_n/P$, where $P$ fixes one $k$-dimensional subspace.
Non-example: $SL_2/T$ with $T$ the diagonal torus is affine and not projective, so it is not a flag variety.

steps: Fix $k<n$ and keep only the subspace $V_k$ of a flag.
The set of all $k$-dimensional subspaces of $V$ is the [Grassmannian](c:grassmannian).
It is the quotient $G/P$ for the stabilizer $P$ of one $k$-dimensional subspace.
So the Grassmannian is a flag variety of partial flags with one step.
links.why: The Grassmannian is the simplest partial flag variety, and results on flag varieties specialize to it.

steps: Take flags with one proper subspace, a line $V_1\subset V$.
The set of lines in $V$ is the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb P(V)$.
It is the quotient $GL(V)/P$ where $P$ is the stabilizer of a line.
links.why: Projective space is the flag variety of lines, so the Borel-Weil theorem for flag varieties contains the case of projective space.

steps: Embed each Grassmannian of $V_i$ in a projective space by the Plücker embedding.
A flag is a point of the product of these spaces where the incidences $V_i\subset V_{i+1}$ hold, and these are polynomial equations.
So the flag variety is a closed subvariety of a product of projective spaces, and the Segre embedding makes it projective.
links.why: Flag varieties are projective, so they are complete and results on projective varieties apply to them.

reminder: A flow network is a directed graph with a source, a sink and a capacity on every edge.
definition: A flow network is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) $G=(V,E)$ with two distinct [vertices](c:vertex) $s$ (the source) and $t$ (the sink) and a capacity $c:E\to[0,\infty)$ on the [edges](c:edge). A flow on it is a function $f:E\to[0,\infty)$ with $f(e)\le c(e)$ for every edge and with inflow equal to outflow at every vertex other than $s$ and $t$.
examples: A pipe system is a flow network. The junctions are vertices, the pipes are edges, and the capacities are the largest flow rates.
Take edges $sa,sb,ab,at,bt$ with capacities $3,2,1,2,3$. Sending $3,2,1,2,3$ along them is a flow of value $5$.
A bipartite matching problem becomes a flow network by adding a source and a sink and giving every edge capacity $1$.
Non-example: a directed graph with an edge of capacity $-1$ is not a flow network, because capacities are not negative.

steps: Take a flow network $(V,E,s,t,c)$.
Forget the source, the sink and the capacities.
What remains is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) $(V,E)$.
The flow network adds two distinguished vertices and a nonnegative capacity on every edge.
links.why: Path and cut arguments for directed graphs apply to flow networks, which add capacities to measure how much flow passes.

reminder: A Fock space is the direct sum of all symmetric or antisymmetric tensor powers of a Hilbert space.
definition: The bosonic Fock space of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is the [completion](c:completion) of $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathrm{Sym}^nH$, where $\mathrm{Sym}^nH$ is the degree-$n$ part of the [symmetric algebra](c:symmetric-algebra) of $H$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^0H=\mathbb C$ holds the vacuum vector. The fermionic Fock space uses the degree-$n$ parts $\Lambda^nH$ of the [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) instead. It describes states of any number of identical particles, each with states in $H$.
examples: For $H=\mathbb C$ (one mode), the bosonic Fock space has the orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle,\dots$ of number states of the harmonic oscillator.
For $H=\mathbb C^n$, the fermionic Fock space is $\bigoplus_{k=0}^n\Lambda^k\mathbb C^n$, which has dimension $2^n$.
Non-example: the tensor power $H\otimes H$ alone is not a Fock space. It holds states of exactly two particles and has no vacuum or other particle numbers.

steps: Take $H=\mathbb C^n$, so $\mathrm{Sym}^kH$ is the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $k$ in $z_1,\dots,z_n$.
Hence $\bigoplus_k\mathrm{Sym}^kH$ is the space of all polynomials in $z$.
The monomials are orthogonal for the Gaussian norm $\int|f|^2e^{-|z|^2}$.
The completion is the [Bargmann-Fock space](c:bargmann-fock-space) of holomorphic functions with finite Gaussian norm.
links.why: The Bargmann-Fock space is a concrete model of the Fock space of $\mathbb C^n$ by holomorphic functions.

reminder: FOLDS is a form of first-order logic in which a sort can depend on elements of other sorts.
definition: FOLDS, first-order logic with dependent sorts, is a form of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) in which a sort can depend on elements of other sorts, as a [dependent type](c:dependent-type) depends on a term. For example, the sort of morphisms from $x$ to $y$ in a [category](c:category) depends on the two objects $x$ and $y$. Equality is weak: it compares only two elements of one sort over the same arguments.
examples: The language of categories has a sort $O$ of objects and a sort $M(x,y)$ of morphisms from $x$ to $y$ for each pair of objects.
A FOLDS formula can say that $f:x\to y$ is an isomorphism, by quantifying over $g\in M(y,x)$ whose two composites are identities.
Non-example: the statement $f=g$ for $f\in M(x,y)$ and $g\in M(x',y')$ with different arguments is not a FOLDS formula, because it compares elements of different sorts.

reminder: A formal proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an axiom or following from earlier ones by a rule.
definition: In a [deductive system](c:deductive-system), a formal proof of a [formula](c:formula) $\varphi$ from a set $\Gamma$ of hypotheses is a finite sequence of formulas that ends with $\varphi$. Each formula in the sequence is an [axiom](c:axiom), a member of $\Gamma$, or a consequence of earlier formulas by a rule of inference.
examples: In a Hilbert system with axiom schemes A1 and A2 and modus ponens, the formula $p\to p$ has a formal proof of five formulas.
The sequence $p$, $p\to q$, $q$ is a formal proof of $q$ from the hypotheses $\{p,p\to q\}$, where the last step is modus ponens.
Non-example: the argument "it is clear that $\varphi$ holds by symmetry" is a proof in daily mathematics but not a formal proof, because it names no axiom or rule for each step.

steps: A [proof](c:proof) is an argument that establishes a statement from accepted assumptions.
A formal proof writes the argument as a finite sequence of formulas.
Each step must be an axiom, a hypothesis or an application of a stated rule, so a program can check it.
So every formal proof is a proof, with a fixed syntax added.
links.why: A formal proof is the checkable form of a proof, so theorems of logic apply to what a proof can establish.

reminder: The free abelian group on a set $S$ consists of formal integer combinations of the elements of $S$.
definition: The free abelian group $\mathbb Z[S]$ on a [set](c:set) $S$ is the [abelian group](c:abelian-group) of finite formal sums $\sum_{s\in S}n_ss$ with integers $n_s$, almost all zero. The set $S$ is a [basis](c:basis) of it, and it has this [universal property](c:universal-property): every map from $S$ to an abelian group $A$ extends uniquely to a group homomorphism $\mathbb Z[S]\to A$.
examples: For a set $S$ with $n$ elements, $\mathbb Z[S]\cong\mathbb Z^n$. For a set with one element, it is $\mathbb Z$.
The additive group of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Z[x]$ is free abelian on the monomials $1,x,x^2,\dots$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is not free abelian, because $2\cdot1=0$ is a nontrivial relation on its only generator.

steps: Take the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor) $U$ from abelian groups to sets.
Send a set $S$ to $\mathbb Z[S]$ together with the inclusion $S\to U\mathbb Z[S]$.
By the universal property, every map $S\to UA$ factors uniquely through a homomorphism $\mathbb Z[S]\to A$.
So $\mathbb Z[S]$ is the [free object](c:free-object) on $S$ among abelian groups.
links.why: The free abelian group is the free object for abelian groups, so a learner can use the same universal property as for free groups and modules.

steps: A [free module](c:free-module) over a ring $R$ is an $R$-module with a basis.
Take $R=\mathbb Z$, and note that $\mathbb Z$-modules are the same as abelian groups.
So a free $\mathbb Z$-module is an abelian group with a basis, which is a free abelian group.
links.why: Results on free modules, such as invariance of rank, hold for free abelian groups.

reminder: A function of exponential type is an entire function with $|f(z)|\le Ae^{\tau|z|}$ for some constants $A$ and $\tau$.
definition: An [entire function](c:entire-function) $f$ has exponential type if there are constants $A,\tau\ge0$ with $|f(z)|\le Ae^{\tau|z|}$ for all $z\in\mathbb C$, where $e^{\tau|z|}$ is the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) of $\tau|z|$. The type of $f$ is the infimum of such $\tau$, that is $\limsup_{r\to\infty}r^{-1}\log\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$.
examples: Every polynomial has exponential type $0$, and $e^{az}$ has type $|a|$.
The functions $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ have exponential type $1$.
For $\phi\in L^1[-a,a]$, the function $z\mapsto\int_{-a}^a\phi(t)e^{izt}\,dt$ has exponential type at most $a$.
Non-example: $e^{z^2}$ is entire but not of exponential type, because $e^{x^2}$ grows faster than $e^{\tau x}$ on the real axis for every $\tau$.

steps: Take a function $f$ of exponential type.
By definition, $f$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function).
Exponential type adds the growth bound $|f(z)|\le Ae^{\tau|z|}$, which general entire functions such as $e^{z^2}$ do not satisfy.
links.why: The growth bound lets a learner control zeros and Fourier transforms, as in the Paley-Wiener theorem.

steps: Take a polynomial $p$ of degree $d$.
There is $C$ with $|p(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^d$ for all $z$.
For every $\epsilon>0$ there is $A_\epsilon$ with $C(1+|z|)^d\le A_\epsilon e^{\epsilon|z|}$.
So $p$ has exponential type $0$, and exponential type also allows functions such as $e^{iz}$.
links.why: Polynomials are the type-zero examples, so exponential type is a growth class that contains them.

reminder: The functional derivative of a functional $F$ is the function that gives the change of $F$ under each small variation of its argument.
definition: Let $F$ be a [functional](c:functional) on functions $\varphi$ on a domain $\Omega$. Its functional derivative at $\varphi$ is the function $\frac{\delta F}{\delta\varphi}$ for which the [derivative](c:derivative) $\frac{d}{d\epsilon}F[\varphi+\epsilon\eta]\big|_{\epsilon=0}$ equals the [integral](c:integral) $\int_\Omega\frac{\delta F}{\delta\varphi}(x)\,\eta(x)\,dx$ for every [test function](c:test-function) $\eta$.
examples: For $F[\varphi]=\int\varphi(x)^2\,dx$, the functional derivative is $2\varphi(x)$.

For $F[\varphi]=\int L(x,\varphi,\varphi')\,dx$, one gets $\frac{\partial L}{\partial\varphi}-\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\varphi'}$, so critical points satisfy the [Euler-Lagrange equation](c:euler-lagrange-equation).
For $F[\varphi]=\varphi(x_0)$, the functional derivative is the Dirac delta $\delta(x-x_0)$.
Non-example: $F[\varphi]=\sup_x|\varphi(x)|$ has no functional derivative at a function with two maximum points, because its first variation is not linear in $\eta$.

steps: Take a finite domain $\Omega=\{1,\dots,n\}$ with counting measure.
A function $\varphi$ is a vector $(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n)$, and $F$ is a function on $\mathbb R^n$.
The integral becomes the sum $\sum_i\frac{\delta F}{\delta\varphi_i}\eta_i$, so $\frac{\delta F}{\delta\varphi_i}=\partial F/\partial\varphi_i$.
So the functional derivative is the [gradient](c:gradient), extended to infinitely many variables.
links.why: A learner can read the functional derivative as the gradient of a function of infinitely many variables.

steps: Take a functional $F$ that is [Fréchet differentiable](c:frechet-derivative) at $\varphi$ on a space of functions.
Its derivative $DF(\varphi)$ is a continuous linear functional on that space.
When $DF(\varphi)(\eta)=\int g\,\eta\,dx$ for a function $g$, then $g$ is the functional derivative.
The functional derivative adds that the derivative is represented by a function.
links.why: The functional derivative is the Fréchet derivative written as a function, which is the form used in the Euler-Lagrange equation.

reminder: The fundamental class of a closed connected oriented manifold is the generator of its top homology group given by the orientation.
definition: Let $M$ be a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $n$ that is [connected](c:connected-space) and oriented. Then $H_n(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, and the fundamental class $[M]$ is the generator of this [homology](c:homology) group that restricts to the chosen local orientation in $H_n(M,M\setminus\{x\};\mathbb Z)$ at every point $x$. For a smooth $M$, integration of top-degree forms over $M$ is evaluation on $[M]$.
examples: For the circle $S^1$, the class $[S^1]$ is the class of the loop that goes once around counterclockwise.
For the sphere $S^2$ with its standard orientation, $[S^2]$ generates $H_2(S^2)=\mathbb Z$, and the opposite orientation gives $-[S^2]$.
For a closed orientable surface $\Sigma_g$ of genus $g$ with a chosen orientation, $[\Sigma_g]$ generates $H_2(\Sigma_g;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$.
Non-example: the projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and the Klein bottle have no integral fundamental class, because they are not orientable and $H_2(-;\mathbb Z)=0$. They have only a class modulo $2$.

reminder: A $G$-CW complex is a $G$-space built by attaching cells of the form $G/H\times D^n$ in order of dimension.
definition: Let $G$ be a [topological group](c:topological-group). A $G$-CW complex is a space $X$ with a continuous [action](c:group-action) of $G$ and a filtration $\emptyset=X_{-1}\subset X_0\subset X_1\subset\cdots$ with union $X$ and the colimit topology. Each $X_n$ arises from $X_{n-1}$ by attaching cells $G/H\times D^n$ along $G$-maps $G/H\times S^{n-1}\to X_{n-1}$, where $G/H$ is an [orbit](c:orbit) type for a closed subgroup $H$.
examples: A [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is a $G$-CW complex for the trivial group $G$, where every cell is an ordinary disk.
The circle $S^1$ with $G=\mathbb Z/2$ acting by $z\mapsto\bar z$ is a $G$-CW complex with two fixed points $G/G\times D^0$ and one free cell $G\times D^1$.
Every smooth manifold with a smooth action of a compact Lie group has a $G$-CW structure, by equivariant triangulation.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ with the trivial action is not a $G$-CW complex, because a $0$-dimensional CW complex is discrete.

steps: Take a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$ and the trivial group $G=\{e\}$.
The only quotient is $G/G=\{e\}$, so a cell $G/H\times D^n$ is an ordinary cell $D^n$.
So a $G$-CW complex for trivial $G$ is a CW complex.
For nontrivial $G$, each cell also carries an orbit type $G/H$.
links.why: Equivariant homotopy theory repeats the cellular constructions of ordinary homotopy theory, with orbits $G/H$ in place of points.

reminder: The Gamma function extends the factorial: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ and $\Gamma(s+1)=s\,\Gamma(s)$.
definition: For $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, $\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$, an [improper integral](c:improper-integral) of a power times the [exponential function](c:exponential-function). It extends by [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) to a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) on $\mathbb C$ with simple poles at $s=0,-1,-2,\dots$ and no zeros.
examples: $\Gamma(1)=1$, and $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for every integer $n\ge0$.
$\Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi$.
At $s=-n$ the function $\Gamma$ has a simple pole with residue $(-1)^n/n!$.
Non-example: $\Gamma(0)$ is not a number. The integral $\int_0^\infty t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ diverges at $t=0$, and $0$ is a pole.

steps: Integrate by parts to get $\Gamma(s+1)=s\,\Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$.
Compute the value $\Gamma(1)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\,dt=1$ directly.
By induction, $\Gamma(n+1)=n\,\Gamma(n)=n!$ for every integer $n\ge0$.
So $\Gamma$ matches the [factorial](c:factorial) at the integers and also has values at other complex numbers.
links.why: A learner can use $\Gamma$ to give meaning to $x!$ for non-integer $x$ and to prove identities for factorials by analysis.

reminder: A gauge symmetry is a transformation of fields that depends on the point of spacetime and leaves the action unchanged.
definition: A gauge symmetry of a field theory with [action functional](c:action-functional) $S$ is a [group](c:group) of local transformations of the fields, with parameters that are functions on [spacetime](c:spacetime), such that $S$ is invariant. Fields that differ by a [gauge transformation](c:gauge-transformation) describe the same physical state, so gauge symmetry is a redundancy of the description.
examples: In electromagnetism, $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ for a function $\lambda$ leaves the field strength $F=dA$ and the action unchanged.
In Yang-Mills theory with a compact group $G$, each smooth map $M\to G$ acts on the connection by a gauge transformation, and the action is invariant.
In general relativity, diffeomorphisms of spacetime act on the metric and leave the Einstein-Hilbert action invariant.

Non-example: rotating all fields of a scalar theory by one constant angle is a global symmetry, because the angle does not depend on the point. It relates different physical states and carries a Noether charge.

steps: Take a gauge symmetry of a theory with [Lagrangian](c:lagrangian) density $L$.
Each transformation leaves the action unchanged, so it is a symmetry of $L$ up to a total derivative.
A gauge symmetry adds that the parameters are functions on spacetime and that transformed fields describe the same state.
links.why: Noether's theorems apply to gauge symmetries as symmetries of the Lagrangian, and the second theorem gives identities among the field equations.

reminder: A generating set of a group is a subset such that every element is a finite product of its elements and their inverses.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $S$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ is a generating set when the smallest [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$ that contains $S$ is $G$ itself. Equivalently, every element of $G$ is a finite product of elements of $S$ and their inverses. The same word is used for modules, rings and other structures, with the matching notion of substructure.
examples: The set $\{1\}$ generates $\mathbb Z$, and $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ generates $\mathbb Z^2$.
The adjacent transpositions $(1\,2),(2\,3),\dots,(n{-}1\ n)$ generate the symmetric group $S_n$.
Every group $G$ is a generating set of itself.
Non-example: $\{2\}$ does not generate $\mathbb Z$, because the subgroup it generates is the set of even integers.

steps: Take a [basis](c:basis) $B$ of a vector space $V$.
Every vector of $V$ is a linear combination of $B$, so $B$ generates $V$ as a module.
So $B$ is a generating set of $V$.
A basis adds that $B$ is linearly independent.
links.why: Many facts about bases only use that the set generates, so they hold for every generating set.

reminder: A spacetime is geodesically incomplete when some maximal geodesic has finite affine length in at least one direction.
definition: A [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $(M,g)$ is geodesically incomplete when some [maximal geodesic](c:maximal-geodesic) $\gamma:(a,b)\to M$ has an affine parameter with $(a,b)\ne\mathbb R$. The [geodesic](c:geodesic) cannot be extended, so a free particle or light ray leaves the spacetime in finite parameter time.
examples: Minkowski space with the origin removed is geodesically incomplete, because a straight line through the origin reaches the missing point at finite affine parameter.
In the Schwarzschild solution, infalling timelike geodesics reach the singularity $r=0$ in finite proper time.
In the expanding Friedmann models, past-directed timelike geodesics end at the big bang in finite proper time.
Non-example: Minkowski space is geodesically complete, because every geodesic is a straight line defined for all values of the affine parameter.

reminder: The GNS construction turns a state on a C*-algebra into a cyclic representation on a Hilbert space.
definition: Let $\varphi$ be a [state](c:state-on-a-star-algebra) on a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$. Put $\langle a,b\rangle=\varphi(b^*a)$ on $A$, divide by the null space $\{a:\varphi(a^*a)=0\}$, and complete to a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H_\varphi$. The algebra acts on $H_\varphi$ by left multiplication $\pi_\varphi(a)[b]=[ab]$, and the class $\Omega=[1]$ of the unit is a cyclic vector with $\varphi(a)=\langle\pi_\varphi(a)\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
examples: For $A=C(X)$ with $X$ compact and $\varphi(f)=\int f\,d\mu$, the construction gives multiplication operators on $L^2(X,\mu)$ with $\Omega=1$.
For $A=M_n(\mathbb C)$ and the normalized trace $\varphi=\operatorname{tr}/n$, the space $H_\varphi$ is $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.
For $A=M_n(\mathbb C)$ and $\varphi(a)=\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle$ with a unit vector $\xi$, the construction gives the defining representation on $\mathbb C^n$ with $\Omega=\xi$.
Non-example: the functional $\varphi(a)=-\operatorname{tr}(a)$ on $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is not positive, so $\langle a,a\rangle<0$ for some $a$ and the construction fails.

reminder: The gradient of a scalar function is the vector of its partial derivatives, pointing in the direction of steepest increase.
definition: For a [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, the gradient is the [vector](c:vector) $\nabla f=(\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_n)$ of [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative). It is the unique vector with $D_vf(p)=\nabla f(p)\cdot v$ for every direction $v$, where the dot is the [inner product](c:inner-product-space).
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, $\nabla f=(2x,2y)$, which points away from the origin.
For $f(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz$, $\nabla f=(a,b,c)$ at every point.
At a point where $\nabla f\ne0$, the gradient is orthogonal to the level set of $f$.
Non-example: $f(x)=|x|$ has no gradient at $0$, because it is not differentiable there.

steps: Take $n=1$, so $f$ is a real function of one variable.
The only partial derivative is $f'(x)$, so $\nabla f(x)=(f'(x))$.
So for $n=1$ the gradient is the [derivative](c:derivative), as a vector with one component.
For larger $n$ it collects one derivative for each coordinate direction.
links.why: The gradient extends the slope of a graph to several variables, and it keeps the meaning of the derivative as a rate of change.

steps: The [differential](c:differential) $df_p$ is the linear map $v\mapsto D_vf(p)$.
On $\mathbb R^n$ with its inner product, each linear map to $\mathbb R$ has the form $v\mapsto w\cdot v$ for a unique vector $w$.
The gradient is this vector $w$ for $df_p$.
So the gradient is the differential after vectors and covectors are identified by the inner product.
links.why: This link shows that the gradient depends on the inner product, while the differential does not.

reminder: The graph of a function $f:X\to Y$ is the set of pairs $(x,f(x))$ in $X\times Y$.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f:X\to Y$, the graph of $f$ is the [subset](c:subset) $\Gamma_f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}$ of the [cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $X\times Y$. A subset $\Gamma\subseteq X\times Y$ is the graph of a function exactly when each $x\in X$ lies in exactly one pair $(x,y)\in\Gamma$.
examples: The graph of $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is the parabola $\{(x,x^2)\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$.
The graph of the identity map of $X$ is the diagonal $\{(x,x):x\in X\}$ in $X\times X$.
The graph of the function $1\mapsto a$, $2\mapsto b$ from $\{1,2\}$ to $\{a,b\}$ is $\{(1,a),(2,b)\}$.
Non-example: the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$ is not the graph of a function $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, because $x=0$ lies in two pairs and $x=2$ lies in none.

steps: A [relation](c:relation) from $X$ to $Y$ is a subset of $X\times Y$.
The graph $\Gamma_f$ is a subset of $X\times Y$, so it is a relation.
It adds the condition that each $x\in X$ is related to exactly one $y\in Y$.
links.why: A function is a special relation, so the graph lets a learner treat functions as sets of pairs.

reminder: The group of units of a ring is the group of its invertible elements under multiplication.
definition: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with identity, the group of units is the set $R^\times$ of [invertible elements](c:invertible) $u$ of $R$, which means $uv=vu=1$ for some $v\in R$. With the multiplication of $R$, it is a [group](c:group), because products and inverses of units are units.
examples: $\mathbb Z^\times=\{1,-1\}$.
For a field $k$, $k^\times=k\setminus\{0\}$. For the matrix ring $M_n(k)$, the group of units is $GL_n(k)$.
$(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$.
Non-example: the number $2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb Z$, because no integer $v$ has $2v=1$. The nonzero integers do not form a group under multiplication.

steps: Take a field $k$ and the ring $R=M_n(k)$ of $n\times n$ matrices.
A matrix is a unit of $R$ exactly when it has an inverse matrix, that is, when its determinant is nonzero.
So $R^\times$ is the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL_n(k)$.
The group of units gives the same construction for every ring $R$, and for $n=1$ it is $GL_1(R)$.
links.why: The group of units extends the idea of invertible matrices to every ring.

reminder: A morphism $i$ has the left lifting property against $p$ when every commutative square from $i$ to $p$ has a diagonal filler.
definition: In a [category](c:category), a morphism $i:A\to B$ has the left lifting property with respect to a morphism $p:X\to Y$, and $p$ has the right lifting property with respect to $i$, when the following holds. For all $u:A\to X$ and $v:B\to Y$ with $pu=vi$, a [commutative square](c:commutative-diagram), there is $h:B\to X$ with $hi=u$ and $ph=v$. Such a map $h$ is a lift or diagonal filler.
examples: In $\mathrm{Set}$, a map $p$ has the right lifting property against $\varnothing\to\{*\}$ exactly when $p$ is a [surjection](c:surjection).
In $\mathrm{Set}$, a map $p$ is injective exactly when it has the right lifting property against the fold map $\{*\}\sqcup\{*\}\to\{*\}$.
In $\mathrm{Top}$, a map has the right lifting property against all inclusions $X\times\{0\}\to X\times[0,1]$ exactly when it is a Hurewicz fibration.
Non-example: in $\mathrm{Set}$, the map $\varnothing\to\{*\}$ does not have the left lifting property against itself, because no map $\{*\}\to\varnothing$ exists to fill the square.

steps: In $\mathrm{Set}$, take $i:\varnothing\to\{*\}$ and a map $p:X\to Y$.
A square from $i$ to $p$ is a point $y\in Y$, because the map $\varnothing\to X$ is unique.
A diagonal filler is a point $x\in X$ with $p(x)=y$.
So $p$ has the right lifting property against $i$ exactly when $p$ is a [surjection](c:surjection).
links.why: Surjectivity is a lifting property, so lifting properties express conditions on maps without naming elements.

steps: Take the horn inclusion $\Lambda^n_k\to\Delta^n$ of simplicial sets.
A square from it to $p:X\to Y$ is a horn in $X$ together with a simplex of $Y$ that fills its image.
A diagonal filler is a simplex of $X$ that fills the horn and lies over that simplex.
So $p$ is a [Kan fibration](c:kan-fibration) exactly when it has the right lifting property against all horn inclusions.
links.why: Kan fibrations are defined by one lifting condition, which is the pattern used for fibrations in every model category.

reminder: A split coequalizer is a coequalizer of a parallel pair, given with splittings that make it preserved by every functor.
definition: Let $f,g:A\to B$ be a parallel pair in a [category](c:category). A split coequalizer of the pair is a [fork](c:fork) $e:B\to C$ with $ef=eg$, together with morphisms $s:C\to B$ and $t:B\to A$ such that $es=\mathrm{id}_C$, $ft=\mathrm{id}_B$ and $gt=se$. Then $e$ is a [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of $f$ and $g$, and $s$ is a [section](c:section) of $e$.
examples: Every algebra $(A,a)$ of a [monad](c:monad) $T$ has the split coequalizer $T^2A\rightrightarrows TA\to A$ given by $Ta$, $\mu_A$ and $a$.
Take a retraction $e:B\to C$ with section $s$. The pair $\mathrm{id}_B$, $se:B\to B$ has the split coequalizer $e$, with $t=\mathrm{id}_B$.
Non-example: the pair $f,g:\{0\}\to\{0,1\}$ with $f(0)=0$ and $g(0)=1$ has the coequalizer $\{0,1\}\to\{*\}$, but it is not split. A map $t:\{0,1\}\to\{0\}$ with $ft=\mathrm{id}$ does not exist.

steps: Take a split coequalizer $e:B\to C$ of $f,g:A\to B$.
Let $h:B\to D$ satisfy $hf=hg$; then $hse=hgt=hft=h$, so $h$ factors through $e$ as $h=(hs)e$.
The factorization is unique, because $e$ has a section $s$ and so is a split epimorphism.
So $e$ is a [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of $f$ and $g$.
links.why: Split coequalizers are the coequalizers that every functor preserves, which is why they appear in monadicity theorems.

reminder: The Hecke algebra of a group $G$ and a subgroup $H$ is the algebra of $G$-endomorphisms of the permutation representation on $G/H$.
definition: For a finite [group](c:group) $G$ and a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$, the Hecke algebra $\mathcal H(G,H)$ is the algebra $\operatorname{End}_G(\mathbb C[G/H])$ of $G$-equivariant endomorphisms of the [permutation representation](c:permutation-representation) on $G/H$. Equivalently, it is the algebra of functions $G\to\mathbb C$ that are constant on each [double coset](c:double-coset) $HgH$, with [convolution](c:convolution) as product. For a locally compact group and a compact open subgroup $H$, one uses compactly supported functions in the same way.
examples: For $H=\{e\}$, the Hecke algebra is the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $\mathbb C[G]$.
For $G=S_n$ and $H=S_{n-1}$, the set $G/H$ has $n$ points, and $\mathcal H(G,H)$ has dimension $2$, because there are two double cosets.
For $G=GL_n(\mathbb F_q)$ and $H$ the Borel subgroup, $\mathcal H(G,H)$ is the [Iwahori-Hecke algebra](c:iwahori-hecke-algebra) of the symmetric group $S_n$ with parameter $q$.
Non-example: for $G=S_3$ acting on $\{1,2,3\}$, the matrix unit $E_{12}$ is an endomorphism of $\mathbb C^3$ but not $G$-equivariant, so it is not in $\mathcal H(G,H)$.

steps: Take $H=\{e\}$, so $G/H=G$ and $\mathbb C[G/H]$ is the regular representation $\mathbb C[G]$.
A $G$-equivariant endomorphism of $\mathbb C[G]$ is determined by the image of the basis vector $e$.
That image can be any element of $\mathbb C[G]$, and composition becomes multiplication, up to the opposite order.
So $\mathcal H(G,\{e\})$ is isomorphic to the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $\mathbb C[G]$.
links.why: The Hecke algebra replaces the group algebra by a smaller algebra that sees only the double cosets of $H$.

steps: The permutation representation $\mathbb C[G/H]$ is an object of the category of $G$-representations.
Its [endomorphism ring](c:endomorphism-ring) in that category is $\operatorname{End}_G(\mathbb C[G/H])$.
This ring is the Hecke algebra, an endomorphism ring with the extra condition of $G$-equivariance.
links.why: The Hecke algebra is the commutant of $G$ on $\mathbb C[G/H]$, so its representations decompose the permutation representation.

reminder: The Hessian of a function is the symmetric bilinear form given by its second partial derivatives.
definition: For a twice [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, the Hessian at $p$ is the symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $(u,v)\mapsto\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}(p)\,u_iv_j$, whose matrix has the second [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) as entries. At a [critical point](c:critical-point) of a function on a manifold, it is a well-defined form on the [tangent space](c:tangent-space), independent of coordinates.
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2+3y^2$, the Hessian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}$ at every point.
For $f=x^2-y^2$, the Hessian at the critical point $0$ is $\operatorname{diag}(2,-2)$. It is nondegenerate with one positive and one negative eigenvalue, so $0$ is a saddle.
For $f(x)=x^3$, the Hessian at $0$ is the zero matrix, so $0$ is a degenerate critical point.
Non-example: away from critical points on a manifold, the matrix of second partial derivatives depends on the chart, so it does not define a bilinear form on the tangent space.

steps: Take $n=1$, so $f$ is a function of one variable.
The Hessian matrix has the single entry $f''(x)$.
The Hessian form is $(u,v)\mapsto f''(x)\,uv$.
So for $n=1$ the Hessian is the [second derivative](c:second-derivative).
links.why: The Hessian carries the second derivative test to several variables, where the signs of its eigenvalues decide the type of a critical point.

steps: At a point $p$, the formula $(u,v)\mapsto\sum_{i,j}f_{ij}(p)u_iv_j$ is linear in $u$ and linear in $v$.
So it is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on $\mathbb R^n$.
It is symmetric, because mixed partial derivatives commute for $C^2$ functions, and this is the added condition.
links.why: Tools for symmetric bilinear forms, such as signature and diagonalization, apply to the Hessian.

reminder: The Hilbert symbol $(a,b)$ is $1$ if $ax^2+by^2=z^2$ has a nonzero solution in the local field, and $-1$ otherwise.
definition: Let $K$ be a [local field](c:local-field) of characteristic $0$, such as $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb Q_p$, and let $a,b\in K^\times$. The Hilbert symbol $(a,b)_K$ is $1$ if the equation $ax^2+by^2=z^2$, given by a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form), has a solution $(x,y,z)\ne(0,0,0)$ in $K^3$, and $-1$ otherwise. It is symmetric in $a$ and $b$ and multiplicative in each of them.
examples: Over $\mathbb R$, $(a,b)_\infty=-1$ exactly when $a<0$ and $b<0$.
Over $\mathbb Q_p$ with $p$ odd, $(a,p)_p=\left(\frac ap\right)$ for a $p$-adic unit $a$, where the right side is the [Legendre symbol](c:legendre-symbol).
For every $a$, $(a,1)_K=1$ and $(a,-a)_K=1$.
Non-example: the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac ap\right)$ has one argument and values in a finite field, so it is not a Hilbert symbol, although it appears in the formula for $(a,p)_p$.

reminder: The Hodge decomposition splits the complex cohomology of a compact Kähler manifold into groups $H^{p,q}$ with $p+q$ equal to the degree.
definition: Let $X$ be a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold). Its [singular cohomology](c:singular-cohomology) splits as $H^k(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X)$, where $H^{p,q}(X)$ is the [Dolbeault cohomology](c:dolbeault-cohomology) group, which is also the space of [harmonic forms](c:harmonic-differential-form) of type $(p,q)$. Complex conjugation maps $H^{p,q}$ onto $H^{q,p}$.
examples: For a complex torus $\mathbb C/\Lambda$, $H^1(\mathbb C/\Lambda,\mathbb C)=H^{1,0}\oplus H^{0,1}$, and each summand has dimension $1$.
For $\mathbb{CP}^n$, $H^{2k}=H^{k,k}\cong\mathbb C$ for $0\le k\le n$, and all other groups $H^{p,q}$ vanish.
For a compact Riemann surface of genus $g$, $H^1=H^{1,0}\oplus H^{0,1}$, and each summand has dimension $g$.

Non-example: the Hopf surface $S^1\times S^3$ is a compact complex manifold but not Kähler. Its first Betti number $1$ is odd, so $H^1$ cannot split as $H^{1,0}\oplus H^{0,1}$ with conjugate summands.

steps: Take a compact Kähler manifold $X$ and the lattice $H=H^k(X,\mathbb Z)$ modulo torsion.
By the Hodge decomposition, $H\otimes\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X)$.
Because $H$ is real, the conjugate of $H^{p,q}$ is $H^{q,p}$.
So $H$ is a [Hodge structure](c:hodge-structure) of weight $k$.
links.why: The Hodge decomposition gives the standard source of Hodge structures, which are then studied without the manifold.

reminder: A homomorphic image of an algebra $A$ is an algebra $B$ with a surjective homomorphism $A\to B$.
definition: Let $A$ be an [algebraic structure](c:algebraic-structure), such as a group or a ring. A homomorphic image of $A$ is a structure $B$ of the same type for which there is a [surjective](c:surjection) [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) $h:A\to B$. Equivalently, $B$ is isomorphic to the quotient of $A$ by a [congruence](c:congruence).
examples: The ring $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphic image of the ring $\mathbb Z$, by reduction modulo $n$.
The image $h(A)$ of any homomorphism $h:A\to C$ is a homomorphic image of $A$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z$ is not a homomorphic image of $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, because the image of a group of order $2$ has at most $2$ elements.

steps: Take a group $G$ with a normal subgroup $N$ and the quotient map $q:G\to G/N$.
The map $q$ is a surjective homomorphism.
So the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/N$ is a homomorphic image of $G$.
By the first isomorphism theorem, every homomorphic image of a group has this form.
links.why: Homomorphic images extend the quotient construction from groups to every algebraic structure, as in Birkhoff's theorem on varieties.

reminder: A hyperbolic 3-manifold is a 3-manifold with a complete Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$.
definition: A hyperbolic 3-manifold is a connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$ with a complete [Riemannian metric](c:riemannian-manifold) of constant [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) $-1$. Equivalently, an orientable $M$ is a quotient $\mathbb H^3/\Gamma$ by a torsion-free discrete subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$.
examples: Hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^3$, the upper half-space with metric $(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2)/z^2$, is the simply connected hyperbolic 3-manifold.
The complement of the figure-eight knot in $S^3$ has a complete hyperbolic metric of finite volume.
The Weeks manifold is a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold of volume about $0.9427$.
Non-example: $\mathbb H^3$ minus a point has constant curvature $-1$ but is not complete. The flat torus $T^3$ is complete but has curvature $0$.

steps: A [hyperbolic manifold](c:hyperbolic-manifold) is a manifold with a complete metric of constant curvature $-1$, in any dimension.
Now fix the dimension to be $3$.
A hyperbolic 3-manifold is a hyperbolic manifold of dimension $3$.
links.why: The general theory of hyperbolic manifolds applies in dimension three, where Mostow rigidity makes the geometry an invariant of the topology.

steps: Take a hyperbolic 3-manifold $(M,g)$.
By definition, $g$ is a Riemannian metric, so $(M,g)$ is a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold).
The hyperbolic case adds dimension $3$, completeness of $g$ and constant sectional curvature $-1$.
links.why: Riemannian tools such as geodesics and volume apply, and the constant curvature makes them explicit.

reminder: A hyperbolic surface is a surface with a complete Riemannian metric of constant curvature $-1$.
definition: A hyperbolic surface is a connected [surface](c:surface) with a complete [Riemannian metric](c:riemannian-manifold) of constant [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) $-1$. Equivalently, an orientable one is a quotient $\mathbb H^2/\Gamma$ of the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane) by a torsion-free discrete subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$.
examples: The hyperbolic plane, for example the upper half-plane with metric $(dx^2+dy^2)/y^2$, is a hyperbolic surface.
Every closed orientable surface of genus $g\ge2$ carries a hyperbolic metric.
The thrice-punctured sphere $\mathbb H/\Gamma(2)$ is a complete hyperbolic surface of finite area $2\pi$.
Non-example: the flat torus has curvature $0$. The modular surface $\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ is a hyperbolic orbifold with cone points, not a surface.

steps: A [hyperbolic manifold](c:hyperbolic-manifold) is a manifold with a complete metric of constant curvature $-1$, in any dimension.
Now fix the dimension to be $2$.
A hyperbolic surface is a hyperbolic manifold of dimension $2$.
links.why: General facts about hyperbolic manifolds hold for surfaces, and in dimension two the metrics form Teichmüller space.

steps: Take the trivial group $\Gamma=\{e\}$.
Then $\mathbb H^2/\Gamma=\mathbb H^2$, which is complete with constant curvature $-1$.
So the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane) is a hyperbolic surface, namely the simply connected one.
Other hyperbolic surfaces are quotients by nontrivial groups.
links.why: Every hyperbolic surface is covered by the hyperbolic plane, so questions about surfaces reduce to the plane and the group $\Gamma$.

reminder: A hyperplane section of a projective variety is its intersection with a hyperplane of the ambient projective space.
definition: Let $X$ be a [projective variety](c:projective-variety) in the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb P^n$ and let $H$ be a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) in $\mathbb P^n$, the zero set of one linear form. The hyperplane section of $X$ by $H$ is the [intersection](c:intersection) $X\cap H$. Its dimension is $\dim X-1$ when $H$ contains no component of $X$.
examples: A plane section of a smooth cubic surface in $\mathbb P^3$ is a plane cubic curve, which may be singular.
A line section of a conic in $\mathbb P^2$ is two points, or one double point when the line is tangent.
A hyperplane section of $\mathbb P^n$ is a copy of $\mathbb P^{n-1}$.
Non-example: the intersection of a surface $X\subset\mathbb P^3$ with a quadric surface is not a hyperplane section, because a quadric is not a hyperplane.

steps: An [intersection](c:intersection) of two sets contains the elements that lie in both.
Take the sets $X$ and $H$ inside $\mathbb P^n$.
The intersection $X\cap H$ is the hyperplane section.
It adds that $X$ is a projective variety and that $H$ is the zero set of one linear form.
links.why: Hyperplane sections let a learner cut a variety down one dimension at a time, as in the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem.
